verses.text: Yahweh showed me, and behold, two baskets of figs set before Yahweh’s temple, after that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the princes of Judah, with the craftsmen and smiths, from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon.
One basket had very good figs, like the figs that are first-ripe; and the other basket had very bad figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad.
Then Yahweh asked me, “What do you see, Jeremiah?” I said, “Figs. The good figs are very good, and the bad are very bad, so bad that can’t be eaten.”
Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,
“Yahweh, the God of Israel says: ‘Like these good figs, so will I regard the captives of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good.
For I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them again to this land. I will build them, and not pull them down. I will plant them, and not pluck them up.
I will give them a heart to know me, that I am Yahweh: and they shall be my people, and I will be their God; for they shall return to me with their whole heart.

“‘As the bad figs, which can’t be eaten, they are so bad,’ surely Yahweh says, ‘So I will give up Zedekiah the king of Judah, and his princes, and the remnant of Jerusalem, who remain in this land, and those who dwell in the land of Egypt.
I will even give them up to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth for evil; to be a reproach and a proverb, a taunt and a curse, in all places where I shall drive them.
I will send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, among them, until they be consumed from off the land that I gave to them and to their fathers.’”

footnotes.content: Two baskets sit before the temple—one held good figs, one rotten. What caught my eye here was Jeremiah's task: to look. The exile is already underway; Nebuchadnezzar has taken the king and the craftsmen to Babylon. But the Lord shows the prophet a sign he can actually see, can hold with his eyes, to help him understand what's coming for those left behind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The contrast could not be sharper: one basket clearly good, ripe, wholesome; the other spoiled beyond recovery. I think of how the Lord sees us at our clearest moments—not hiding what is good, not glossing over what has rotted. He doesn't lie about the state of things. That honesty itself is a mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah sees plainly what is placed before him: good figs, bad figs. When the Lord asks 'What do you see?' He's inviting the prophet to name it. There's something steadying in being asked to look truth in the eye and say its name. The vision won't hide what's spoiled, and Jeremiah won't either.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hinge moment: 'Yahweh's word came to me.' After the vision, comes the word. The sign points toward meaning. A prophet's work is to hold the sign and wait for the word to give it shape. Sometimes we too must learn this patience—to see first, then listen for what the Lord means to teach us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the first word: the good figs are the captives sent into exile. Not left behind in the wreckage—sent out by the Lord Himself 'for good.' What an inversion! Those torn from home, those carried away, are called good. Exile becomes the place where God intends goodness. I think of how He sometimes must take us far from where we felt safe to refine us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's eyes are set on them 'for good'—and He speaks not of punishment but of restoration: build them, not tear them down; plant them, not uproot. The language shifts from judgment to covenant promise. This is the teacher speaking of the student after exile refines them—stern because He loves, but always looking toward their return.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will give them a heart to know Me. Not just knowledge, but a changed heart—the kind of knowing that means turning back 'with your whole heart.' The exile's purpose, then, is not merely punishment but transformation: the Lord Himself will make them His people again, from the inside out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the bad figs: Zedekiah, the king who remained behind, and the princes and remnant still in Jerusalem, and those who fled to Egypt. They were not carried away; they stayed in the wreckage and refused exile. The Lord says: these I will give up. To remain in the world without Him becomes its own kind of ruin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this scattering—the casting about 'among all the kingdoms of the earth for evil.' We know exile, displacement, wandering, the weight of being an outsider. And we know too the temptation to think such scattering means God has abandoned us. But the vision shows: dispersal without His eye upon you is the curse; dispersal with His covenant is redemption.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sword, famine, pestilence—the three plagues. Those who refused the mercy of exile and exile's refining will consume themselves where they stand. This is not the Lord's wrath alone, but the natural end of turning away from Him. The vision closes with separation made plain: good figs restored, bad figs destroyed. The choice always lies before us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
